articles.title: Operationalizing health equity: a mixed-methods approach to measuring organizational capacity in public health practice
articles.authors: Mazzucca-Ragan S, Jacob R, Luke D, Malone S, Valko C, Brownson R.
articles.content:
## Introduction

Health equity is a core function for public health practice (1–3). The imperative of a health equity approach is driven in part by decades of rising income inequality (4), the visibility and impacts of historic structural racism (5), and the need to view public health as a common good rather than a commodity (6). It involves moving beyond simply measuring health disparities to ensuring every individual has a fair and just opportunity to be healthy (7). An aim of advancing health equity is making health a shared societal responsibility. The concept is evident in national, state, and local strategic plans, as well as in the notion of Public Health 3.0, where local leaders are “public health strategists” who influence the social determinants of health through partnerships across multiple sectors (e.g., education, transportation, justice, housing) (1).

To support progress tracking, public health agencies are guided by the axiom: “what gets measured, gets done (8).” Many public health agencies support their measurement function using surveillance systems for certain health conditions or risk factors (e.g., disease registries, ongoing surveys of behavioral risk factors, hospital discharge data). Additionally, agencies have traditionally invested resources in developing and implementing monitoring systems for community and health outcomes. These data can be supplemented with various indices of social deprivation (e.g., area deprivation index, social deprivation index). Several public health systems [e.g., the King County determinants of equity data tool (9)] have developed equity-relevant datasets (e.g., on education, economic development, employment, and criminal justice) (10).

Despite its importance, there are limited data on the extent to which public health agencies are comprehensively addressing health equity. A broader data ecosystem is needed to measure not only community-level indicators but also awareness, skills, leadership, and performance within public health agencies and work units. In a 2016 nationwide survey of US practitioners in state health departments, only 2% reported working primarily on health equity, and 9% reported that health equity was one of their multiple priority areas (11). National data collected in 2017 showed that more than half of public health agency staff believe their agencies should be very involved in improving health equity, yet few reported being very involved in addressing specific social determinants of health (e.g., transportation, housing) (12). In a more recent (2022) study on health equity practices among state public health practitioners (13), the strongest areas were the staff's ability to describe the causes of health inequities (82% agreeing or strongly agreeing) and to identify disparities within their jurisdictions (82%). Only 32% of respondents reported having systems in place to track progress on health equity.

Efforts to measure organizational, rather than community, capacity for equity are not new, though they remain fragmented. A scoping review of indicators available to Ontario local public health agencies found few that were evidence-based or validated, and concluded that those worth retaining needed substantial further definition before use (14). Guidance developed during the COVID-19 pandemic took a different route, appending health equity prompts to an existing set of public health emergency preparedness indicators so that agencies would articulate equity considerations at each stage of organizational decision-making (15). Most recently, a scoping review identified 17 organizational health equity capacity assessments for public health organizations and found limited evidence on how these tools had been implemented and what they yielded (16). The present study advances this literature in three respects. First, practitioners generated the domains rather than deriving them from expert consensus or document review. Second, the resulting items were subjected to confirmatory factor analysis in a national sample, yielding evidence of internal structure and reliability. Third, the instrument measures capacity at the work unit level, where staff time, data, and partnerships are largely allocated.

The overall goal of the current study was to develop a new set of health equity measures for public health practice, using best practices in measurement development (17–21). We accomplished our goal with three activities, in which we: (1) conducted concept mapping (22) to identify priority health equity domains, (2) developed a survey instrument, with cognitive testing, to measure these core domains, and (3) conducted a national survey of public health practitioners to perform confirmatory factor analysis and assess the measurement structure of the instrument.

## Methods

This study was approved by the Washington University in St. Louis Institutional Review Board (IRB# 202506181).

### Mixed-methods participatory input

Concept mapping is a mixed-methods, participatory approach used to gather and organize ideas through several steps: develop the focus prompt; identify participants; generate ideas; structure ideas; analyze data and create visual representations; and interpret and use results (23). GroupWisdom, a web-based concept mapping software, was used throughout the process.

#### Statement generation (brainstorming)

Statement generation was conducted in December 2024. Participants included program staff and leadership from state and local public health departments. Contact lists were obtained from our organizational partners, i.e., the Big Cities Health Coalition, the Missouri Public Health Institute, the National Association of Chronic Disease Directors, and the de Beaumont Foundation. A total of 315 individuals were invited to participate. After removing invalid email addresses, bounce-backs, and individuals no longer in their positions, 295 were eligible.

Participants accepted a written consent statement in the software and were then asked to complete the focus prompt with as many statements as they desired. Participants responded to the prompt: “For a public health agency to advance health equity, it needs…” All previously generated statements were visible to participants, and statements were anonymous. A total of 201 unique statements were generated. The research team reviewed the statements to remove redundancies and consolidate conceptually similar responses. Through iterative discussion and consensus, the list was reduced to 82 unique statements, which were carried forward to the sorting and rating steps. The statement list was finalized in alignment with concept mapping best practices, which recommend limiting the sorting and rating phases to fewer than 100 unique statements (24).

#### Sorting and rating

Sorting and rating were conducted between January and February 2025. A total of 299 individuals (eligible from Phase 1 and additional contacts that were recommended by participants) were invited to participate; 290 were deemed eligible after invalid or ineligible contacts were removed. Participants sorted the 82 statements into groups that they identified as conceptually meaningful and assigned a name to each group. They could create as many or as few groupings as they wanted. Each statement could appear in only one pile, and no statement could be sorted into its own separate pile. Following this task, participants rated each statement separately on two dimensions, importance and feasibility, using a 7-point Likert scale (1 = low; 7 = high). Importance and feasibility ratings were used to characterize participants' views of each statement and were not used to select or prioritize domains. All eight clusters were carried forward into instrument development.

#### Cluster analysis and map solution

The GroupWisdom platform organizes the sorted data using several quantitative methods applied sequentially. A similarity matrix is created first to consolidate the sorting data from all participants. Then, multidimensional scaling is used to create a point map in which each statement is represented as a point on a two-dimensional plane (25, 26). Distances between points reflect how often statements were sorted together; points that are closer together are interpreted as more conceptually similar. Hierarchical cluster analysis is used to group points representing similar concepts (27, 28). Of the 56 participants who completed the rating activities, 53 produced valid sorts, meaning the participant placed every statement into a group, created more than one group but fewer groups than the total number of statements, and did not place any statement in a group by itself. All 53 valid sorts were included in the cluster analysis; all 56 participants were included in the importance and feasibility analyses. The research team examined cluster maps of four to 15 cluster solutions to determine which best reflected the point map and were most interpretable. Each cluster map was evaluated for the consistency of ideas and using the statistics reported by GroupWisdom. The statistics evaluated were the multidimensional scaling stress value, which indexes how closely the two-dimensional point map reproduces the original sorting data; bridging values for each statement, which indicate whether a statement was sorted consistently with the statements nearest to it on the map (values near 0) or bridged separate regions of the map (values near 1); and the number of statements assigned to each cluster across candidate solutions. Cluster solutions that split conceptually cohesive groups or produced clusters too broad to label were rejected.

Ratings of each statement were averaged, and an overall cluster average was calculated. A ladder graph was produced in GroupWisdom to visualize and compare the cluster-level averages for the importance and feasibility ratings. Additionally, a “Go-Zone” map was created that assigns each statement to one of the two ratings, creating a priority-quadrant plot to guide future efforts to advance health equity in public health practice.

Based on coherence and interpretability of the clusters, the research team selected the eight-cluster solution as the best-fitting model. Following member checking with participants, minor refinements were made to cluster labels and item assignments, in accordance with standard concept mapping practices. The final eight clusters were: (1) Funding (5 items); (2) Agency Practices (11 items); (3) Communication (7 items); (4) Data Practices (16 items); (5) Organizational Partnerships (10 items); (6) Community Representation (14 items); (7) Leadership (7 items); and 8) Staff Development (12 items). These clusters informed the development of the subsequent survey instrument.

### Instrument development and psychometric assessment

#### Instrument development

Using best practices for item development, the survey items were derived directly from the concept mapping results and from two previous surveys (11, 13, 21). The research team met to review the concept mapping statements and ratings and to develop an initial set of survey items that best reflected the priority areas in each domain. Statements were edited according to measurement development processes, for example, removing double-barreled items. Following development of the pilot tool, the team conducted cognitive testing of the survey with public health professionals (N = 6) to assess clarity, relevance, and interpretability (29). One round of revisions took place to incorporate cognitive interview feedback prior to administering the survey.

The initial instrument included 47 items organized into eight sections (five to seven items per section) corresponding to the concept mapping clusters. All 47 initial items, and the model in which each removed item was dropped, are listed in Table S2. The start of the instrument included the directions: “Please indicate how often each of the following activities has occurred at your work unit over the past 12 months.” Response options were measured on a 6-point Likert scale (1 = Almost never; 6 = Almost always) with an option for “Not able to answer”. Five or more statements per section were selected at this stage to allow for removal of poorly performing items after initial testing, using the criteria described below.

#### Pilot sample and data collection

A random sample of 1,416 individuals was drawn from our partner organizations' membership list and individuals who participated in the concept mapping process, to ensure representation of practitioners and partners with expertise in chronic disease prevention and familiarity with the equity-related constructs being measured. An additional 12 individuals were added through self-nomination or colleague recommendations to capture relevant expertise not reflected in the membership list, bringing the total to 1,428 invitations distributed via email in August 2025.

Five reminder emails were sent to non-respondents over an eight-week period. The survey closed in October 2025. After removing invalid email addresses and automated replies indicating extended leave or separation from the agency, 1,295 individuals were deemed eligible. Of those, 234 completed the survey, yielding an 18% response rate. Respondents represented 53 U.S. states and territories.

#### Analyses and model fit evaluation

Data were managed and analyzed in R. We conducted descriptive analyses, visualization, and psychometric analyses. We used the psych package in R to calculate measures of internal consistency (reliability), including Cronbach's alpha (30).

Confirmatory factor analysis was conducted to assess the fit of the proposed eight-factor model using the lavaan R package (31). The base model was specified with one factor and all 47 items from the survey using a robust maximum likelihood (MLR) estimator and full information maximum likelihood (FIML) to handle missing data. Responses of “Not able to answer” were recoded as missing and handled under FIML alongside item nonresponse. Missing responses accounted for 3.7% of all item responses. Items were considered poorly performing and were candidates for removal if they cross-loaded onto other factors based on modification indices, e.g., when the highest modification indices included one item and factors in which the item was not originally placed. Additionally, items that were highly correlated with another item (>0.7) were considered for removal; in such cases, the item that had the stronger factor loading was retained.

Model fit was evaluated using multiple indices, including the chi-square test of model fit, Comparative Fit Index (CFI), Tucker-Lewis Index (TLI), Root Mean Square Error of Approximation (RMSEA), and Standardized Root Mean Square Residual (SRMR). Although a non-significant chi-square test (p > 0.05) indicates good model fit, this test is highly sensitive to large sample sizes. Therefore, additional fit indices were emphasized. CFI and TLI values range from 0 to 1, with values ≥0.90 indicating acceptable fit and ≥0.95 indicating good fit. RMSEA values < 0.05 indicate close fit, values between 0.05 and 0.08 indicate reasonable fit, and values ≥0.10 indicate poor fit (32, 33). Confidence intervals around RMSEA were examined to assess approximate model fit. SRMR values were also evaluated, with thresholds similar to RMSEA and less sensitivity to sample size.

## Results

### Mixed-methods participatory input

#### Participants

Seventy-three participants completed the statement generation activity (25% response rate). Fifty-six participants completed the rating tasks (19% response rate), and 53 of these produced valid sorts. Across the concept mapping steps, participants represented 35 U.S. states and six U.S. territories. In the brainstorming step, 56% of respondents were from local health departments and 33% from state health departments (Table 1). Similarly, in the sorting and rating steps, 54% were from local and 39% from state health departments. Participants had substantial professional experience, with a mean of 13.5 years (SD = 10.2) and 12.7 years (SD = 8.7) in their current role for the brainstorming and sorting/rating steps, respectively.

> **Table 1. Participant characteristics, health equity in public health practice, United States, 2025.**

| Characteristic | Concept mapping phase 1 (N = 73) | Concept mapping phase 2 (N = 56) |
|---|---|---|
| Organization |  |  |

| State health department | 24 (33%) | 22 (39%) |
| Other categories with N = 3 or less | 8 (11%) | 4 (7%) |

| Role |  |  |
| Program manager or coordinator | 18 (25%) | 17 (31%) |
| Department head | 10 (14%) | 10 (19%) |
| Epidemiologist | 7 (10%) | 6 (11%) |
| Health equity/health disparities coordinator | 6 (8%) | 4 (7%) |
| Health educator | 3 (4%) | 2 (4%) |
| Other categories with N = 2 or less | 29 (39%) | 15 (28%) |
| Equity in their work\* |  |  |
| A small portion (1–24%) | 7 (9%) | 7 (13%) |
| Some portion (25–49%) | 14 (19%) | 11 (20%) |
| A significant portion (50–74%) | 26 (36%) | 14 (25%) |
| Nearly all (75–100%) | 26 (36%) | 24 (43%) |

| Yes | 31 (42%) | 25 (45%) |

Respondents represented a range of professional roles. In the brainstorming step, the most common roles were program manager/coordinator (25%), department head (14%), and epidemiologist (10%). Participants who sorted and rated were similarly distributed, with program managers/coordinators (31%) and department heads (19%) most frequently represented. More than 70% of participants reported that at least half of their work addressed health equity or health disparities, and approximately half identified as members of a historically underrepresented population in research.

#### Concept map

Sorting analyses yielded an eight-cluster solution that was retained based on interpretability and statistical fit (stress index = 0.228). The stress index is a goodness-of-fit statistic produced by multidimensional scaling that quantifies the discrepancy between the two-dimensional point map and participants' original sorting data. It ranges from 0 to 1, and lower values indicate that the map represents the sorting data more faithfully. In a pooled analysis of 69 concept mapping studies, stress values averaged 0.28 and ranged from 0.17 to 0.34; the value observed here falls below that average, indicating good fit (24). The final clusters were (1) Funding, (2) Agency Practices, (3) Communication, (4) Data Practices, (5) Organizational Partnerships, (6) Community Representation, (7) Leadership, and (8) Staff Development (Figure 1, Table S1).

> Figure 1. Cluster map, health equity in public health practice.

#### Importance and feasibility ratings

Across clusters, statements were generally rated highly for importance (means largely ≥5.4 on a 7-point scale), while feasibility ratings were more variable (Figure S1). Several statements fell into the high-importance/high-feasibility quadrant (Quadrant I; Figure S2), including fostering collaboration across sectors and incorporating social determinants of health into equity efforts. In contrast, several items were rated highly important but less feasible (Quadrant IV), including ensuring sufficient funding and fostering political leadership at multiple levels. Overall, participants consistently rated structural, systems-level, and partnership-oriented strategies as highly important, with feasibility varying depending on resource and political considerations (Figures S1, S2).

### Instrument development

#### Descriptive statistics and internal consistency

A total of 234 respondents completed the survey (18% response rate). Respondents represented 53 U.S. states and territories. The initial 47-item survey was organized into eight factors aligned with the concept mapping clusters (Table S2).

#### Confirmatory factor analysis

The eight-factor structure derived from the concept mapping exercise was supported by the pilot data. Model fit indices are presented in Table 2. The baseline one-factor model demonstrated poor fit (CFI = 0.701; TLI = 0.687; RMSEA = 0.096; SRMR = 0.072). The hypothesized eight-factor full model improved fit (CFI = 0.826; TLI = 0.813; RMSEA = 0.074; SRMR = 0.067), though indices remained below established thresholds for good fit.

> **Table 2. Summary of model fit indices, health equity in public health practice, United States, 2025.**

Two reduced models were tested. The first, a reduced model (40 items) further improved model fit (CFI = 0.866; TLI = 0.853; RMSEA = 0.071; SRMR = 0.062). The final model (32 items) demonstrated the best overall fit, meeting or approaching recommended thresholds (CFI = 0.908; TLI = 0.896; RMSEA = 0.066; SRMR = 0.051). Although chi-square statistics were statistically significant across all models, this was expected given sample size sensitivity.

### Final survey domains, items, and measurement properties

The eight-factor, 32-item model was retained as the final survey measure, as it demonstrated the best balance of statistical fit and conceptual relevance (Table 3). Conceptual relevance was evident in that all eight domains identified through concept mapping were retained in the final model, each represented by four items, so that item reduction did not eliminate any practitioner-identified domain. The retained items also preserved the substantive content of each domain. Leadership, for example, retained items covering accountability, systemic change, and political navigation, and Data Practices retained items covering progress tracking, evaluation, presentation of data to varied audiences, and attention to specific subgroups. Mean item scores ranged from 3.73 to 5.49 on a 6-point scale, indicating moderate to high frequency of reported activities.

> **Table 3. Survey domains and items, health equity in public health practice.**

“Not able to answer” responses varied across domains. In the final instrument, these responses were least common for Organizational Partnerships (0.9%) and Agency Practices (1.2%), and most common for Funding (6.2%) and Leadership (9.4%); the three items drawing the most such responses all belonged to these two domains. Sixty-seven percent of respondents answered every item in the final instrument.

Domain-level means, calculated for each respondent as the mean of their available items within a domain, ranked as follows: Agency Practices (5.27), Data Practices (4.91), Communication (4.84), Organizational Partnerships (4.66), Staff Development (4.63), Leadership (4.41), Community Representation (4.34), and Funding (4.19).

This ranking follows a consistent pattern. Domains describing internally controlled, values-oriented activity scored highest and varied least across respondents: every item in Agency Practices had a mean at or above 5.10 and a standard deviation below 1.00, the narrowest spread of any domain. Domains that depend on resources, political conditions, or the redistribution of authority scored lowest and varied most. Funding, Leadership, and Community Representation each contained items with standard deviations above 1.20, and four of the five lowest-scoring items in the instrument fall within these domains: using economic evaluation data in decision-making (M = 3.73), maintaining sufficient funding for disparity-related priorities (M = 4.06), co-creating solutions with those most impacted by disparities (M = 4.11), and negotiating political challenges (M = 4.14). The fifth, partnerships with businesses (M = 4.05), is described below.

Variation within domains was also informative. Organizational Partnerships spanned the widest range of any domain, from partnerships with nonprofit organizations (M = 5.05) to partnerships with businesses (M = 4.05), suggesting that agencies partner readily within the nonprofit and governmental sectors but engage the private sector far less often. In Community Representation, sharing decision-making authority with partners (M = 4.55) scored higher than co-creating solutions with those most impacted by disparities (M = 4.11). In Leadership, the item on embracing systemic change (M = 4.71) scored higher than the two items involving political risk (M = 4.28 and M = 4.14). Across the instrument, agencies reported doing the work they control more often than the work that requires resources, political cover, or direct involvement of affected communities.

Inter-factor correlations ranged from 0.567 to 0.868 (Table S3). The strongest correlation was observed between Communication and Community Representation (r = 0.868), followed by Data Practices and Staff Development (r = 0.825). Leadership was strongly correlated with Staff Development (r = 0.800) and Community Representation (r = 0.776). Funding demonstrated moderate correlations with all other domains (r range: 0.635–0.680). Organizational Partnerships was the most distinct domain in the model. It had the lowest average correlation with the other seven domains (mean r = 0.65) and the single lowest inter-factor correlation in the matrix, with Leadership (r = 0.567); its correlations with Staff Development (r = 0.607) and Agency Practices (r = 0.613) were also among the lowest observed. This pattern indicates that an agency's external partnership activity is not a simple function of its internal equity infrastructure, and that the two can develop independently. While correlations were substantial, they remained below 0.90, indicating related but distinct constructs.

## Discussion

Integrating stakeholder-driven concept mapping with rigorous psychometric testing, this study establishes a multidimensional measure of foundational characteristics that define a public health agency's capacity to systematically advance health equity. Eight factors were identified through a mixed-methods approach, spanning agencies' internal operations and their integration of community members and organizational partners who are integral to advancing health equity in their communities. This study provides one of the first empirically derived tools to assess equity capacity at the work unit level and moves the field from a conceptual discussion of equity toward operational indicators of capacity. Importantly, this work highlights that advancing health equity requires systems-level organizational change, not isolated programmatic efforts.

Our findings provide empirical evidence that public health practitioners view health equity capacity as a multidimensional organizational system. Rather than focusing on individual programs or isolated policies designed to reduce health disparities, the resulting map suggests that advancing equity requires a complex integration of skills, leadership commitment, and infrastructure woven across a public health agency, similar to other frameworks that align health equity work with the core functions of governmental public health (3). Further, this organizational system does not operate in a vacuum but requires collaboration between public health agencies, their organizational partners, and members of the communities they serve. The focus on external partners in our concept map aligns with Public Health 3.0, which reframes public health practitioners as conveners of cross-sector partnerships and community members and organizations to advance population health (1). By defining these interconnected domains and developing items that measure each domain, our findings move the field toward a concrete, operational roadmap for institutionalizing health equity within the day-to-day functions of public health agencies.

The domains our participants generated correspond to dimensions identified in prior reviews of organizational health equity capacity, including leadership commitment, workforce development, resource allocation, and data infrastructure (16). Where our results depart from that work is in how finely practitioners distinguish the internal conditions supporting equity. In developing indicators for Ontario agencies, expert informants found that items concerning organizational systems and support for equity work did not fit the four groupings used to organize the indicator set (assessing and reporting on health status, modifying programs for priority populations, engaging in multisectoral collaboration, and policy advocacy), prompting the addition of a fifth category encompassing organizational and system development (14). Cohen et al.'s framework of organizational capacity for public health equity action characterizes an organization's internal context through three dimensions: shared values, commitment and will, and organizational infrastructure (34). The examples they give of infrastructure include access to and ability to interpret local data on inequities, advocacy skills among the workforce, and processes ensuring that equity-seeking populations can influence organizational decision-making. These three examples correspond to Data Practices, Staff Development, and Community Representation in our instrument, each of which our analysis supports as a distinct factor. Practitioners appear to treat these internally facing dimensions as separate concepts, which matters for measurement because an agency may be well staffed yet without the data to target its efforts, or data-rich yet unable to bring affected communities into decisions about how that data is used.

The survey results highlight a stark disconnect between high-level organizational values and the operational realities of public health practice. While respondents reported that their units overwhelmingly maintain disparity reduction as a core value (M = 5.49), factors capturing the concrete execution of equity initiatives received substantially lower ratings. Specifically, agencies reported significant difficulty navigating political challenges (M = 4.14), securing dedicated funding (M = 4.06), and authentically co-creating solutions with the communities most impacted by disparities (M = 4.11). This gap suggests that while administrative endorsement is well-established, the field lacks the structural infrastructure necessary to bring affected communities into decision-making and withstand external political pressures (13). These internal capacity deficits are exacerbated by systemic workforce pressures: a lack of demographic representativeness hinders authentic community engagement (35), while the high financial burden of graduate education limits the entry of diverse talent and undermines the sustainability of equity-focused staff development (36). While these broader systemic barriers are beyond the control of any single agency, providing a psychometrically sound method for tracking agency capacity represents a necessary step toward organizational accountability.

The development of this instrument is strengthened by a mixed-methods design that integrated practitioner-driven concept mapping with quantitative validation, ensuring the domains and survey items are both grounded in practice and psychometrically sound. Also, survey respondents represented 53 states and territories, indicating that these concepts are relevant nationwide. Further, the high internal consistency of all eight factors (Cronbach's alphas between 0.79 and 0.91) suggests that the items within each domain are conceptually cohesive and clearly understood by practitioners as distinct organizational constructs.

However, these findings should be considered alongside some limitations. While our sample was geographically and professionally diverse, the modest response rate introduces the potential for nonresponse bias. Because the sampling frame drew on membership lists of organizations focused on chronic disease prevention and equity, and because more than 70% of respondents reported doing equity-related work or belonging to an underrepresented group, respondents were likely more engaged with equity work than the broader public health workforce. Estimates of organizational capacity reported here may reflect an upper bound rather than an average. Additionally, using a self-report format may introduce social desirability bias; however, practitioners' perceptions are the most appropriate metric for these domains. These internal perceptions are the primary drivers of organizational decision-making, the allocation of staff time, and the ultimate development and sustainment of structures that support equity. If social desirability influenced responses, its effect likely varied across domains. Agency Practices, which asks respondents to affirm that their unit holds disparity reduction as a core value and incorporates it into policies and operations, is the domain tied most closely to stated organizational values, and it showed the highest mean and the smallest variance of the eight domains. Domains asking about observable resource and authority conditions, including Funding, Leadership, and Community Representation, showed lower means and substantially wider spread. This is the pattern that would be expected if items closer to organizational values drew more uniformly favorable responses than items closer to operational reality, and it echoes the gap between endorsement of health equity and reported involvement in specific activities found in earlier national surveys (12, 13). The same pattern is also consistent, however, with genuine differences in how difficult these domains are to enact. Distinguishing between the two will require validating the instrument against external indicators such as budget allocations, staffing records, and documented community agreements.

Our measure provides a standardized method for tracking organizational equity characteristics over time. Internally, agencies can use the eight-factor survey to track their own capacity. The concept mapping ratings reported here reflect the views of 56 practitioners at one point in time and should not be treated as a general prioritization scheme; agencies should prioritize based on their own staff and partners' perceptions of importance and feasibility. Standardizing these metrics also provides a rigorous, data-driven foundation for the 'Public Health Capacity Teams' proposed by Bishai and colleagues, who advocate for multisectoral, participatory evaluations of both internal infrastructure and the external capabilities required to operationalize equity in the Public Health 3.0 era (37). Future research should strengthen the tool's psychometric properties by testing predictive validity for community outcomes, sensitivity to change, and performance across diverse agency types. Finally, exploring the tool's utility in restrictive political contexts remains vital.

Comparing the ratings with the survey data shows what practitioners considered important and achievable alongside what their units do, and the two diverge most clearly within Organizational Partnerships. Six of the ten partnership statements fell into the high-importance/high-feasibility quadrant, while none of the Funding or Leadership statements did (Table S1). Practitioners rated partnering with other agencies, fostering collaboration with sectors outside health, and committing to consistent engagement with partners as both important and achievable. Yet the corresponding survey items received only moderate scores (domain mean 4.66), and the domain correlated least strongly with the rest of the instrument. Partnership work is therefore neither contested nor viewed as out of reach, and yet it is not consistently occurring. That combination makes Organizational Partnerships a distinct target for near-term action, and distinguishes it from Funding and Leadership, where low scores accompany low perceived feasibility and the barriers lie largely outside any single agency. Agencies looking for tractable starting points can prioritize partnership development, and particularly partnerships with businesses, which was both the lowest-scoring partnership item (M = 4.05) and an area practitioners rated as feasible. Treating partnership development as a standing element of program planning, rather than a project-specific activity, would convert an area of high perceived feasibility into measurable practice.

The pattern of “Not able to answer” responses points the same direction. Although these responses were infrequent, they differed across domains. Practitioners most often selected “Not able to answer” for items about their unit's leadership and funding conditions, and least often for items about its partnership activity. The domains that scored lowest and were rated least feasible are also the ones respondents most often declined to rate, which is consistent with those conditions being set above the work unit rather than within it. We could not test this directly, since position level was not captured in the pilot survey. The sampling frame suggests most respondents were middle managers and frontline program staff rather than agency executives, which would place funding and leadership decisions above the level at which they work. Capturing position level in future administrations would test this explanation and would also show who within an agency is best positioned to assess which domains.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates that practitioners view equity capacity as a multidimensional organizational system rather than isolated activities. This reliable eight-factor instrument provides a rigorous tool for agencies to assess and strengthen the internal infrastructure required to operationalize health equity. Advancing equity is an ongoing process requiring sustained structural investment, measurable capacity, and the political will to navigate systemic challenges. As practices must adapt to shifting political and funding landscapes, these domains represent a dynamic framework that should evolve with the field. Future efforts should prioritize longitudinal application of this tool to track institutional progress and drive the systemic transformations necessary to improve population health.

Health equity is a core function for public health practice (1–3). The imperative of a health equity approach is driven in part by decades of rising income inequality (4), the visibility and impacts of historic structural racism (5), and the need to view public health as a common good rather than a commodity (6). articles.title: Exploring public health equity in digital access: voices from marginalized groups using the "Mawid" application in Saudi Arabia.
articles.authors: Al-Anezi FM.
articles.content:
## Introduction

The rapid adoption of innovative technologies such as artificial intelligence (AI) within healthcare systems has significantly transformed the delivery and experience of healthcare, particularly in how individuals engage with health services, communicate with healthcare providers, access care, and self-manage their health conditions (1). While technological integration can improve the efficiency and effectiveness of healthcare services, it is equally important to assess whether individuals are prepared and able to adopt and use these systems. This raises important questions regarding equity and inclusion, which are fundamental principles of public health systems globally (2, 3). Digital health innovations should therefore not only improve healthcare efficiency and effectiveness but also ensure that individuals across different social groups, regardless of age, income, education, or geographic location, can benefit from them. Failure to ensure equitable access and participation may reinforce existing structural inequalities in health outcomes (4).

Digital inclusion refers to the ability of individuals and groups to access, understand, and effectively use digital technologies and is increasingly recognized as an important determinant of health equity (5). Conversely, digital exclusion reflects disparities in access to and effective use of digital technologies, including internet connectivity, devices, digital skills, and the ability to navigate complex e-health interfaces (6, 7). The multidimensional nature of the digital divide encompasses broader socioeconomic, geographical, cultural, and psychological inequalities and processes of marginalization (8, 9). Theories of technology-mediated inequality further suggest that when digital tools and applications are not inclusively designed and implemented, their benefits may disproportionately accrue to technologically proficient individuals while creating additional barriers for those with limited digital proficiency or other contextual constraints (10, 11). In healthcare, such disparities may reduce access to timely services and limit individuals’ autonomy in managing their health. Understanding these differential experiences is therefore essential for operationalizing health equity within increasingly digital and AI-enabled health systems.

> **BOX 1. Contributions to the literature.**

| • Shifts digital health assessment beyond usability and adoption toward equity, dignity, privacy, and lived social constraints shaping healthcare access.• Provides qualitative evidence from Saudi Arabia, addressing a regional gap in population health research on digital exclusion.• Informs public health policy by highlighting why uniform digital systems risk widening health inequities without parallel non-digital access pathways |
|---|

Saudi Arabia provides an important context for examining these issues because of its rapid digital transformation of healthcare under Vision 2030 (12). Among the country's digital health initiatives is Mawid, a Ministry of Health application designed to facilitate appointment scheduling, referral management, telehealth consultations, and health education and awareness services (13). The application has achieved substantial population-level reach, with more than 24 million users, representing approximately 68% of the Saudi population (14). However, widespread adoption does not necessarily indicate equitable access or meaningful use across population groups. Older adults, individuals with lower incomes, and residents of rural or less-developed regions may encounter distinct structural, social, cultural, and psychological barriers to using digital health services. These barriers may include limited digital literacy, accessibility challenges, inadequate infrastructure, lack of technical support, and concerns regarding trust and usability. Thus, the high level of adoption of Mawid provides an important basis for examining whether the benefits of digital healthcare are distributed equitably across different population groups.

The concept of the digital divide has consequently evolved beyond simple differences in internet access to encompass digital literacy, usability, accessibility, trust, and the capacity to meaningfully engage with digital health services (15). Previous research has consistently identified older adults, low-income individuals, and rural residents as groups that may experience disproportionate barriers to digital health adoption (16, 17). Among older adults, reduced digital confidence, increased cognitive load, and accessibility limitations may hinder the use of mobile health applications (18). Low-income populations may experience constraints related to reliable internet access, device ownership, and digital health literacy (19), while rural populations may face limitations in digital infrastructure and access to technical support (20). Although digital health platforms can improve healthcare utilization, continuity of care, and patient autonomy among digitally capable users (21), they may simultaneously create barriers for those who are unable to use them effectively, particularly when digital pathways replace rather than complement traditional routes to healthcare access (22). This concern is especially relevant for government-provided digital health services that, although formally voluntary, may become strongly encouraged or functionally necessary for accessing healthcare.

Existing evidence concerning Mawid has largely focused on awareness, usability, satisfaction, and perceived effectiveness. Several studies reported high levels of user satisfaction and usability, particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic (13, 23, 24). However, these findings provide limited insight into whether the application's benefits have been distributed equitably, particularly in the post-pandemic period. Higher awareness of Mawid functionalities has been associated with greater likelihood of use (25), while differences in awareness have been reported according to age, income, employment status, education, and geographic region (25, 26). Older adults, lower-income individuals, and residents of less-developed regions have been reported to demonstrate lower levels of knowledge and independent use and to rely more frequently on family members to access services through the application (26). Although studies have also identified low digital literacy, unreliable internet access, and limited trust as barriers to telehealth adoption among older Saudis (27, 28), geographic isolation and limited primary healthcare infrastructure remain important challenges in rural areas (29, 30). Importantly, much of the existing research has relied on technology acceptance or user-experience frameworks, with comparatively limited application of digital inclusion and health equity perspectives. Consequently, structural barriers related to digital literacy, accessibility, usability, trust, and infrastructure remain insufficiently examined in relation to equitable use of Mawid (25).

Therefore, despite the extensive adoption of Mawid and the growing body of research examining its usability and acceptance, an important knowledge gap remains concerning whether the application supports equitable access and meaningful participation across socially and geographically diverse population groups. In particular, limited evidence is available regarding how marginalized users experience and navigate the platform and which structural and individual-level factors facilitate or constrain their effective use. Addressing this gap is important for ensuring that the ongoing digital transformation of the Saudi healthcare system contributes to, rather than exacerbates, existing health inequalities. Accordingly, this study aims: (1) to examine the extent of digital inclusion and equitable access to the Mawid application among marginalized user groups in Saudi Arabia, including older adults, low-income individuals, and rural residents; and (2) to identify and analyze the key barriers and facilitators affecting these groups’ ability to effectively use the Mawid system, with particular focus on digital literacy, usability, accessibility, and perceived trust in the digital health platform.

## Methods

### Study settings and participants

A descriptive qualitative design was adopted in this study to gain a deeper understanding on digital access and health equity in the use of the Saudi Ministry of Health's Mawid application among underrepresented populations. A qualitative approach is adopted because assessing multi-dimensional constructs such as health equity and digital divide, which is associated with social, cultural, psychological, and technical aspects is complex and context-dependent, which may not be effectively analyzed using quantitative approaches, as they require deeper interpretation of users’ perceptions (31, 32). Therefore, focus group discussions, discussions were adopted in this study, which facilitates in-depth exploration of participants’ lived experiences, perceived barriers, and enabling factors influencing equitable engagement with the Mawid platform. Accordingly, participants were included if they were 50 years of age or older for the older-adult group, or if they belonged to one of the targeted marginalized categories: rural residents, low-income individuals, people with disabilities, or intersectional users. For the purpose of this study, “older adults” were defined as individuals aged 50 years and above. Although international and Saudi policy definitions often use thresholds of 60 or 65 years, several digital-health and technology-adoption studies in Saudi Arabia and similar contexts have used 50 + as a pragmatic cutoff to capture those beginning to experience age-related barriers in accessing eHealth services (33). In developing regions, the WHO has noted that “older adult” may correspond to ages 50–55 and above, reflecting earlier onset of functional aging, chronic conditions, and retirement transitions compared with high-income settings. In the Saudi and broader Gulf context, individuals in their early fifties frequently experience transitions associated with aging, including early retirement, onset of multiple chronic conditions, and reduced digital confidence, which may affect their engagement with digital health platforms (34, 35). In all cases, participants had to have used or attempted to use the Mawid application and possess at least basic familiarity with it. Individuals were excluded if they had never used or attempted to use Mawid, were unable to provide informed consent, or could not meaningfully participate in the focus group discussion because of severe communication, cognitive, or health-related limitations.

### Recruitment and sampling

A purposive sampling strategy (36) was adopted to ensure the inclusion of diverse participants from marginalized groups who could provide rich, context-specific insights into digital access and health equity in relation to the Mawid application. Potential participants were identified and invited through multiple channels to reach older adults, rural residents, low-income individuals, people with disabilities, and users with intersecting vulnerabilities. These channels included primary healthcare centers and clinics in urban, semi-urban, and rural areas; community organizations and social-support groups working with older adults and people with disabilities; and personal and professional networks of the research team. In addition, snowball sampling was used, whereby initial participants were asked to refer other eligible individuals they knew who had used or attempted to use the Mawid application.

Individuals were initially approached by the researcher or a research assistant, who provided a brief verbal explanation of the study and screened for eligibility based on the inclusion criteria: age ≥50 years for the older-adult group; residence in rural or remote areas; self-reported low income; presence of a disability; or a combination of these characteristics, together with having used or attempted to use the Mawid application. Those who expressed interest and met the eligibility criteria were provided with further information about the study and invited to participate in an online focus-group discussion. Participants were not recruited directly through the Mawid application or Ministry of Health databases. Recruitment was conducted independently of the Mawid system, although all participants were required to have some prior experience (actual use or attempted use) of the application. This approach was chosen to avoid restricting participation only to current registered users who actively engage with the system, and to include individuals who had tried but discontinued use.

Variation was sought in gender, age group, educational level, and region to capture diverse perspectives. An estimated sample size of 19 was identified. A final sample of 25 was achieved, who were grouped into five focus groups with five participants in each group. Focus groups were designed to be relatively homogeneous in terms of key demographic characteristics (e.g., age, residence, socioeconomic status, or disability status) to promote open discussion, while heterogeneity was maintained across groups to enable comparative analysis. Data collection continued until data saturation was reached, which occurred after the fifth focus group, as no new themes or substantial new insights emerged in the final discussions.

The recruitment strategy may have introduced some sample bias. Participants were recruited through clinics, community organizations, personal and professional networks, and snowball sampling, which may have favored individuals who already have some level of social connectedness, access to health services, or contact with community structures. Individuals who are completely disconnected from health facilities, community organizations, or social networks may therefore be underrepresented. In addition, because all participants were required to have at least some experience with the Mawid application, the sample does not include people who have never heard of or attempted to use the system. These limitations should be considered when interpreting the findings, particularly regarding the most digitally and socially excluded populations.

### Data collection

Focus group discussions were conducted through secure online video conferencing application from 8/12/2025 to 12/1/2026. Focus group discussions were conducted through a secure online video-conferencing application. This mode of data collection was selected due to the wide geographic dispersion of the target participants across urban, semi-urban, rural, and remote areas, which made in-person meetings logistically challenging and costly. Online discussions also offered greater flexibility in scheduling, reduced travel burdens for participants, and aligned with infection-control considerations in the post-pandemic period. To facilitate participation, individuals received simple written and verbal instructions on how to join the session, and were offered a brief technical check prior to the discussion. Where necessary, participants were allowed to join using a mobile phone with audio-only capability, and some participants were supported by a family member to connect to the session. Average discussion time ranged between 60 to 80 minutes. Discussions were guided by questions focusing on key components, which include the experiences of accessing and using Mawid, perceived usability and satisfaction, barriers to digital access and equity, trust and inclusion, and recommendations for improvement. The discussions were audio-recorded and conducted in Arabic with the consent of participants.

### Data analysis

All focus-group discussions were audio-recorded in Arabic and transcribed verbatim in Arabic by the author. The Arabic transcripts were then translated into English by the author, who is fluent in both Arabic and English. To ensure accuracy and preserve the meaning of participants’ expressions, a two-stage verification process was applied.

First, a bilingual expert independently reviewed all transcripts and compared the English translation against the original Arabic for accuracy, completeness, and nuance. Discrepancies and alternative interpretations were discussed and resolved by consensus, and the agreed approach was then applied consistently to the final English versions.

Second, for key illustrative quotes used in the Results, a back-translation procedure was employed: selected quotes were translated from English back into Arabic by a different bilingual researcher who was not involved in the initial translation. These back-translations were compared with the original Arabic transcripts to check whether the core meaning and emotional tone were preserved. Minor adjustments were made to the English wording where necessary to improve fidelity to the original expressions while maintaining readability. All final quotes used in the manuscript were checked against the original Arabic transcripts to ensure that they accurately reflected participants’ intended meanings.

Thematic analysis, following Braun and Clarke's six-phase framework (37), which includes familiarization, initial coding, theme development, review, definition, and reporting, was used to analyze the focus-group discussion data. An inductive coding approach was used for identifying the themes to naturally emerge from the focus-group discussion data by organizing patterns into codes and sub-codes. NVIVO, V.14 was used for data organization, coding, and theme refinement.

### Ethical considerations

Ethical approval was obtained from the Institutional Review Board of Imam Abdulrahman Bin Faisal University, Saudi Arabia (approval number: IRB-2025-14-0850). The study involved five online focus-group discussions with 25 participants. Before each discussion, participants received information about the study purpose, procedures, potential risks, confidentiality protections, the voluntary nature of participation, and their right to withdraw at any time without consequences. Verbal informed consent was obtained from all participants before data collection and was audio-recorded as part of the study documentation. All procedures were conducted in accordance with the ethical principles of the Declaration of Helsinki.

## Results

Participants reflected a diverse range (see Table A1 in Supplementary File), with each focus group including similar participants; and heterogeneity is maintained across the focus groups. Each focus group is categorically included participants of older adults, rural residents, low-income individuals, people with disabilities, and intersectional users who combined these characteristics respectively. Participants age group ranged from 29 to 71 years; representing both genders from urban, semi-urban, rural, and remote rural settings. Occupations varied across participants, such as retired workers, informal laborers, caregivers, and single parents. Low or uneven digital literacy, unstable work patterns, shared or basic devices, and health or functional limitations was observed among the participants reflecting the marginalized group. Thematic analysis of focus group discussions led to the identification of seven key themes (see Table A2 in Supplementary File), which are presented below.

### Apps as barriers to getting healthcare

The Mawid application was perceived across all focus groups as a barrier or gate that must be successfully crossed in order to receive care, framing access to healthcare as a conditional process dependent on digital competence. Older adults described anxiety and stress when using the application, fearing that a single mistake could lead to lost appointments and longer waiting times.

“One wrong press and the appointment is gone; then you wait again for weeks,” said an older participant (OA2).

“I feel scared to open the app; I always think I will make a mistake and lose my turn,” explained another older woman (OA4).

Low-income participants highlighted that the application disproportionately benefits those with good devices and stable connectivity, while impeding those with limited resources.

“If your phone is old or the net is slow, the app just keeps loading and you miss the appointment time,” said a low-income participant (LI3).

These issues resulted in delayed or irregular care, as users lacked confidence and feared being blamed for errors. Many participants contrasted the app with face-to-face or telephone booking, where they could explain their situation and sense of urgency to a receptionist.

“On the phone you can tell them it is urgent. The app does not listen,” noted a caregiver (LI5).

Participants challenged the notion that digital systems ensure equal treatment, arguing that “equality is not sameness” when starting points are unequal.

### Mismatch between the application design and lived realities

Participants highlighted a clear incompatibility between the application's design logic and their everyday realities in terms of time, work, and health. Low-income participants described frequent trade-offs between clinical attendance and income, as daytime and working-day appointments conflicted with their job schedules.

“The appointment times are for people who sit in offices, not for those who work all day in the heat,” remarked a delivery driver (LI2).

Single parents reported that rigid appointment rules, combined with childcare and school demands, made missed appointments feel like a moral failure rather than a consequence of structural constraints. Older adults with chronic illnesses such as diabetes and hypertension described the multi-step process and small fonts as overwhelming.

“When you are sick and tired, you cannot follow all these steps. The letters are too small,” said an older participant with chronic illness (OA4).

Rural participants noted that farming seasons and long travel times to clinics contradicted with strict booking windows, and that missing an appointment due to network failure or harvest work could have serious health consequences.

“When I am in the field during harvest, I cannot keep checking the phone for messages,” said a rural farmer (RR1).

### Layered infrastructural and contextual barriers

Infrastructural barriers constituted a second layer of exclusion, exacerbating existing geographic and economic disadvantage. Rural participants emphasized that the application is fully dependent on network quality, describing instances of the app hanging, missed notifications, and ambiguous appointment confirmations.

“Sometimes I travel all the way to the clinic, and they say there is no appointment in the system. The app said it was confirmed,” reported a rural participant (RR5).

These issues increased uncertainty and costs, with wasted trips resulting in loss of time, money, and work. Low-income participants noted the need to purchase more advanced mobiles to cope with these issues, adding substantial costs.

“We had to buy a new phone just for the app; for us this is a big cost,” said a low-income caregiver (LI5).

Intersectional participants described the transformation of healthcare access problems from “distance only” to “distance and technology,” reflecting an increased burden (MX1, MX4).

### Reliance on informal support and loss of privacy

Across all focus groups, most participants relied heavily on informal support networks to access the application, including family members, neighbors, friends, co-workers, and occasionally clinical staff. Older adults and people with disabilities often depended on children or siblings to schedule appointments, interpret notifications, and correct errors.

“I have to ask my son to book for me, even for private problems. It is embarrassing,” shared an older man (OA1).

This dependency was experienced as embarrassing and dignity-eroding, as sensitive health information became visible to others. Rural participants described sharing phones and asking for help as a necessity that compromised their privacy.

“I don't like that my Neighbour sees my messages when she helps me. It is not private,” said a rural homemaker (RR2).

Participants distinguished between “informal” support, which was ad hoc and contingent on goodwill, and “structural” support, which they felt should be built into the health system. This dependence on informal networks was linked to fragile trust; participants trusted the government but distrusted the application, which they felt undermined their realities.

### Accessibility, disability, and invisible exclusion

Participants with disabilities viewed accessibility as a major barrier, citing problems with design features. Users with vision problems reported difficulties with small text, poor contrast, and incomplete screen-reader compatibility.

“The letters are too small; even with my glasses I cannot read them,” said a participant with low vision (PD1).

Users with hearing difficulties noted that help materials lacked captions, while those with cognitive or learning challenges highlighted the cognitive load imposed by the multi-step process (PD4, PD5).

“The instructions use difficult medical words; I feel stupid when I don't understand,” reported a participant with low literacy (MX4).

These findings reflected that neutral and standard design features may not fit all users. As a result, disabled participants often relied on family or untrained clinic staff to access services. Participants identified the need for accessibility features such as screen-reader compatibility, adjustable text, simplified language, captions, and assisted booking options, viewing these changes as essential to equity rather than optional enhancements.

### Fragile trust and perceived misalignment of equity

Participants expressed confidence in the government's intentions but raised concerns about the application's ability to provide equitable care. A perceived divide was observed between urban residents, who benefited from stable infrastructure and swift bookings, and rural users facing network failures and travel burdens.

“They think everyone has good internet and a new phone. That is not our life,” said a remote rural participant (RR5).

This misalignment contributed to trust erosion and shaped perceptions of equity. Many participants felt that the application promoted access for the digitally privileged while creating barriers for marginalized users.

“It promotes efficiency, not equity. Those are not the same,” noted a rural participant (RR4).

This theme highlights that trust in digital health applications depends not only on institutional credibility but also on perceived fairness and responsiveness to lived diversity.

### Recommendations for inclusive design

Participants offered practical suggestions reflecting the concept of equity as designing around real lives rather than idealized, stable users. Recommendations included simplified or separate versions of the application for older adults, offline or SMS-based appointment scheduling, grace periods for missed appointments due to connectivity failures, and the preservation of in-person or telephone booking as parallel routes.

“There should be a simple version for old people, with big buttons and clear words,” suggested an older participant (OA3).

“If the net fails, there should be a way to confirm by SMS or phone, not only the app,” proposed a rural resident (RR2).

Some participants recommended community-based digital support points at clinics or neighborhood centers, providing in-person support and training. Findings suggested that true inclusion and health equity require design considerations for diverse user capabilities and circumstances, and warned that eHealth applications risk becoming mechanisms of digital exclusion if they prioritize efficiency over accommodating varied capacities and challenges.

Although most participants described Mawid as a barrier or conditional gatekeeper, a few reported more positive experiences. One older participant with moderate digital skills (OA1) stated that the app “saves time and I do not need to talk to the receptionist,” and preferred digital booking over face-to-face contact. Similarly, one rural school administrator (RR3) with moderate digital skills and a stable connection described the system as “mostly easy” and reported few missed appointments. These deviant cases highlight that digital exclusion is not uniform; individuals with better devices, connectivity, and digital confidence may experience Mawid as convenient rather than exclusionary. Nonetheless, these participants were in the minority, and the dominant pattern across groups was one of conditional access and added burden.

## Discussion

This study provides an understanding on how government facilitated digital health applications operate in practice among the marginalized population in the context of health-equity-centered focus; thereby extending the previous research in such applications like Mawid, which has largely focused on usability, satisfaction, and adoption metrics. Although, previous studies (13, 23–28) reported high acceptance and perceived usefulness of Mawid, mostly during the Covid-19 pandemic period, findings in this study revealed that digital access to healthcare applications function as a conditional gatekeeper for receiving care, disproportionately disadvantaging older adults, rural residents, low-income individuals, and people with disabilities. Therefore, it is evident that digital transformation can unintentionally lead to structural inequalities in certain contexts as marginalized populations, when access routes (requirement of digital skills and awareness) become mandatory rather than complementary (4, 8, 22).

Participants, especially older adults highlighted experiences of fear, anxiety, delayed care, and avoidance behaviors with the Mawid application, suggesting that lack of digital skills and cognitive load can lead to reduced digital confidence, which in turn can affect users engagement and access to care (18, 29). This finding aligns with multidimensional digital divide theories, where exclusion stems not just from access but from usability, literacy, and contextual fit (38–41). Furthermore, the findings in this study reflected that such barriers are not just individual skill deficits, but are reinforced by rigid application design which penalize errors such as delayed care, and removes opportunities for negotiation or explanation, which are essential for marginalized groups, such as older adults. In addition, socio-economic disadvantage was linked to limited digital engagement, particularly among the low-income participants as observed in (19), and further extended this by revealing the hidden costs of digital health applications, especially time poverty, data affordability, and job insecurity, which are rarely captured in previous empirical studies.

Focusing on the rural participants experiences, findings in this study reinforce previous observations in relation to infrastructural inequities and geographic isolation (20, 29, 30), but conceptualizes such barriers as layered exclusions, where digital applications add additional burden on top of existing barriers such as distance-related constraints in healthcare access. One of the key observations was access to healthcare was facilitated by informal support networks such as friends, family, colleagues across all the groups, highlighting the family dependence (26) in Saudi Arabia. However, these findings were extended by revealing that this dependency was viewed as dignity-eroding and privacy-compromising, highlighting an overlooked equity trade-off in digital health adoption.

Furthermore, the findings in this study strongly align with technology-mediated inequality theories (10–12), by reflecting how neutral or common system designs privilege users with digital skills and stable resources; while undermining the marginalized populations’ struggles. It was also observed that trust in Mawid application was largely institutional rather than technological, reflecting that trust is relational and contingent on perceived fairness and responsiveness (7, 28). Overall, the findings suggest that efficiency-driven digitalization risks undermining public health equity unless inclusive design and alternative access pathways are systematically embedded.

### Theoretical and practical implications

Theoretically, this study demonstrates the drawbacks in equality-based digital designs in healthcare by demonstrating that such designs can result in inequitable outcomes, reinforcing technology-mediated inequality theories. The findings reiterate that deficits in digital literacy is a failure in system design, rather than users drawbacks or shortcomings. Furthermore, it reiterates the multidimensional nature of digital divide and health equity factors, where emphasis should be given to both application's efficiency and also the users’ expectations, and accessibility issues. Focusing on the practical implications, the findings reflect the need for operationalizing equity-oriented digital health governance, including parallel non-digital access routes, simplified interfaces for older adults, accessibility-by-default design, and flexible appointment policies. System designers and policy makers should consider the lived experience feedback and the reality on ground, for designing digital health strategies for digital transformation in healthcare, to promote health equity by enhancing access to care, without pre-conditions and undermining marginalized vulnerable populations.

### Study limitations and future research

This study has several limitations. Firstly, the qualitative design and purposive sampling techniques may limit the generalizability of the findings beyond similar marginalized populations in Saudi Arabia. Secondly, data collection using online focus groups may have excluded individuals with the most severe digital access barriers. Although the study specifically targeted marginalized groups, all participants needed a minimum level of digital access (an internet-connected device and sufficient connectivity) and basic digital literacy, or the support of someone who could help them connect, in order to participate. This means that individuals without any reliable internet access, without a suitable device, or with extremely low digital confidence were likely underrepresented or entirely absent from the sample. The findings therefore reflect the experiences of marginalized users who are able to engage at least minimally with digital platforms, rather than those who are completely digitally excluded. Thirdly, data collection using online focus groups may have excluded individuals with the most severe digital access barriers, including those without reliable internet connectivity, appropriate devices, or sufficient digital literacy to participate in video-conferencing. Although the study specifically focused on marginalized groups, participants still needed a minimum level of digital access and support to join the discussions, which may have led to the exclusion of the most digitally excluded individuals. Fourthly, findings are based on self-reported experiences and perceptions, which might be influenced by social desirability and psychological factors. However, the study provides rich, contextual insights that are essential for understanding equity implications, which were often undermined in previous empirical studies. Future studies may adopt quantitative methods focusing specifically on marginalized populations with larger samples to further analyze the health equity dimension in the context of rapid digital transformation in the Saudi Arabian healthcare sector. Mixed-methods designs that combine surveys with in-depth interviews or focus groups could also help capture both the breadth and depth of digital exclusion and its impact on access to care.

## Conclusion

This study has found that the government-managed healthcare applications like Mawid have improved healthcare efficiency, but their equity implications remained uneven. Digital healthcare access for marginalized users is shaped by the intersection of social, economic, geographic, and functional constraints, which has transformed technology into a barrier rather than facilitator of quality and continued care. Therefore, in order to achieve health equity, there is a need to shift from traditional uniform digital health solutions and strategies, to an inclusive, flexible, and human-centered application design. By undermining such adjustments, national digital health applications may reinforce existing inequalities, rather than enabling sustained and enhanced access to quality care, as a part of healthcare digitalization.

However, the equity implications of access to healthcare by such digital health platforms for marginalized populations remain underexplored, especially in the countries which are rapidly transforming their healthcare system through digitalization, such as Saudi Arabia. In this context, this study aims to investigate digital inclusion and health equity among users of the Saudi Ministry of Health's "Mawid" application. Methods A qualitative exploratory design was adopted in this study using five focus groups discussions (25 participants with five participants in each group) as an approach for data collection. Each focus group is categorically included participants of older adults, rural residents, low-income individuals, people with disabilities, and intersectional users who combined these characteristics respectively. Braun and Clarke's thematic analysis framework was used to identify key patterns and themes from the data collected through discussions. Results Findings revealed that Mawid often functioned as a conditional gatekeeper to healthcare, with barriers related to digital literacy, infrastructural constraints, time poverty, and accessibility. Participants relied heavily on informal support networks, frequently at the cost of privacy and autonomy. Uniform system design was perceived to disadvantage users with complex social and health needs. Conclusion Government-managed digital health applications enhances efficiency of healthcare operations, but may reinforce health inequities, if equity-centred digital design and alternative access pathways are not considered in the system design and formulation of digital health strategies.
