### Realist-informed findings

#### Focus groups and coding

Focus group members were drawn from the membership of the Public Health Association of BC. Three different focus group sessions were conducted in order to reach the designated number of participants (N = 12). The number of participants in the focus groups was limited to 12 for two reasons. Twelve represents 24% of the core membership and 8% of the active membership and as such would not detract for later research with the same population and would still meet the demand for theoretical sufficiency vs. saturation (Vasileiou et al., 2018). Two, the minimum sample size for data saturation in qualitative studies indicated by Clark and Braun (2013) was 12. In fact, saturation was achieved with 12 participants as coded results demonstrated consistency in response to thematic analysis.

The first session had four participants, the second session had three participants with one person joining from session 1 to complete the Mentimeter survey, the final session had three participants. Three participants chose to provide their feedback online via the Mentimeter survey. Questions in the Mentimeter survey were designed to solicit opinion and experience from focus group respondents and were the basis for a deeper discussion of context and decision making with regard to the VPC. Given the supportive and pro-social context of PHABC, it was anticipated that members would be motivated to participate in the online Violence Prevention Charter process. Nevertheless, it was necessary to clarify what the motivating mechanism was for participation and why some members chose not to support the VPC.

Both coders reviewed the each other’s findings and, in this process, validated assignment of content within the secondary frame. This process was straightforward and there were no disagreements regarding assignments to the frames. The coders worked independently and those results were then assessed collectively with discussion until unanimous agreement was reached. Figure 4 shows the integrated results of the coding process where context and sentiment were the organized focus of the assessment.

> Figure 4. Focus group-violence prevention charter: context and outcomes – coders 1 and 2. From focus group teleconference meetings, August and December 2019.

The realist-informed inquiry explored the contextual conditions and generative mechanisms underlying participant decisions to engage with the Violence Prevention Charter. Focus groups were undertaken to examine the reasoning behind decisions to sign or decline the Charter and to identify the Context–Mechanism–Outcome (CMO) configurations associated with voluntary participation. Findings from the qualitative inquiry informed development of the subsequent Social Network Analysis survey, providing an opportunity to examine whether the identified mechanisms were evident across the broader PHABC network. This sequential explanatory approach is consistent with realist inquiry, which seeks to explain how interventions work by examining how participants reason and respond to program resources within particular contexts (31, 32). More recent realist scholarship has extended this perspective by emphasizing that mechanisms are not fixed properties of interventions but emerge through the interaction between program resources, participant reasoning, and context, particularly within complex public health systems (33, 34).

#### Context–mechanism–outcome configurations identified through realist-informed qualitative analysis

The focus-group analysis identified three principal generative mechanisms influencing engagement with the Violence Prevention Charter: creation of social good, trust in the source, and influence of colleagues and peers. These mechanisms were identified independently by both coders and were subsequently reconciled through the coding process. Within the social good theme, participants connected their decision-making to the value of violence prevention, advocacy, and a broader moral commitment to public health. One participant described the desired outcome simply as “safety, security and peace for all.”

Trust in the source was similarly prominent. Participants distinguished between online requests originating from organizations they knew and trusted and those from unfamiliar sources. PHABC was described as an “evidence based source,” and its established credibility provided an important context for engagement with the Charter. This reasoning was expressed more fully by one participant:

“It is important for me to have a trusted and known organization that is focusing around the online advocacy.”

The participant explained that although they sometimes engaged in online advocacy, requests from organizations they only vaguely knew generated uncertainty about the purpose and direction of the advocacy. Trust therefore operated through participants’ assessment of the credibility of the organization communicating the request rather than through exposure to the online message alone.

The third mechanism was influence from colleagues and peers. Participants referred to PHABC colleagues, organizational relationships, conference participation, and prior exposure to violence-prevention activities when explaining their decision to support the Charter. One participant identified a violence-prevention workshop at a PHABC conference as contributing to their decision to sign, while others reported signing following encouragement from a PHABC colleague. The coding therefore situated peer influence within an existing professional social network rather than as a generalized effect of social media.

The CMO analysis also identified contextual conditions that could inhibit engagement even where participants were supportive of violence prevention. Participants who had not signed described overflowing inboxes, competing demands on their time, the need for reminders, unfamiliar online solicitations, and concerns about subsequent requests for donations. One participant described this constraint directly:

“I think it’s a time issue, by the time I go through Facebook and email and all messages regarding my friend who advocate for this and that and I feel I’ve used my time that way, so it’s a time issue for me.”

This response is important because non-adoption did not necessarily indicate disagreement with the Charter or its violence-prevention objectives. Rather, practical conditions could prevent an otherwise supportive individual from acting on the invitation. Participants indicated that barriers such as time, competing online communication and lack of follow-up could potentially be overcome through reminders or communication from a trusted organization.

Participants also differentiated online advocacy from other forms of public-health action. One participant described using social media selectively for issues operating at a broader scale:

“I use social media very erratically; I tend to do the social media and a group of things and I was worried I was getting lazy and not getting involved in the more local activist things and so I am using social media for issues I care about on a national or provincial scale.”

This illustrates the agency involved in participants’ decisions about whether and how to engage digitally. Although all focus-group participants reported being at least somewhat comfortable with social media, they did not describe themselves as regular users, reinforcing the distinction between technological capability and a decision to participate in online advocacy.

The resulting CMO configuration therefore suggests that voluntary adoption occurred when the Charter’s violence-prevention purpose aligned with participants’ existing public-health values, the request was communicated through a credible and trusted source, and professional relationships reinforced its relevance. Conversely, competing demands, uncertainty regarding online requests, and characteristics of the digital environment could interrupt engagement despite underlying support for violence prevention. The principal outcomes were decisions to adopt or decline the Charter and subsequent willingness to share or advocate for its principles. These qualitative findings subsequently informed the Social Network Analysis questions examining trust and professional influence across the broader PHABC network.

Participants consistently identified creation of social good, trust in shared information, influence of colleagues and peers, and professional commitment to violence prevention as the principal generative mechanisms influencing engagement with the Violence Prevention Charter.

These mechanisms were activated within contexts characterized by established professional relationships, organizational credibility, alignment with shared public health values, and confidence in the sponsoring organizations. Consistent with realist methodology, these mechanisms reflected participants’ reasoning in response to contextual conditions rather than attributes of the intervention itself (31, 35). This interpretation aligns with Shaw et al. (34), who argue that mechanisms should be understood as the reasoning and responses triggered when participants interact with program resources under particular contextual conditions. The mechanisms identified in the present study reflect this conceptualization, demonstrating that trust, professional influence, commitment to violence prevention, and the creation of social good emerged through participants’ interpretation of the intervention rather than from the intervention itself.

The contextual conditions influencing these mechanisms included participants’ familiarity with the Violence Prevention Charter, existing professional relationships, organizational roles, and confidence in the credibility of the information being communicated. Within these contexts, trust and professional influence acted as generative mechanisms supporting voluntary engagement, while competing priorities, uncertainty regarding the initiative, and limited familiarity with the Charter reduced the likelihood of participation. These findings demonstrate that engagement was shaped by participants’ reasoning within their professional context rather than by exposure to online communications alone. Similar findings have been reported in contemporary realist evaluations of complex health interventions, where differences in implementation are explained through variations in stakeholder reasoning and local context rather than through differences in the intervention itself (36). Jagosh (33) likewise argues that understanding how mechanisms are activated across diverse contexts provides a more meaningful explanation of program outcomes than describing implementation processes alone.

The principal outcomes included decisions to adopt or decline the Violence Prevention Charter, willingness to share Charter information with colleagues, and varying levels of advocacy and organizational engagement. Importantly, the subsequent Social Network Analysis demonstrated high levels of trust and professional influence across the PHABC network, providing empirical support for the mechanisms identified through the focus groups. Together, the qualitative and quantitative findings demonstrated that voluntary adoption resulted from the interaction between contextual conditions and generative mechanisms rather than from the intervention alone.

Taken together, the realist-informed findings provided the explanatory link between the observed patterns of diffusion and organizational network structure. While diffusion modeling demonstrated the timing and trajectory of dissemination, and Social Network Analysis characterized the professional relationships through which information travelled, the realist-informed inquiry explained the reasoning underlying participants’ decisions to engage with the Violence Prevention Charter. These complementary findings provide the basis for the integrated interpretation presented in the Discussion.

## Discussion

### Integrated interpretation of the findings

This study integrated web analytics, Bass diffusion modeling, Social Network Analysis (SNA), and a realist-informed examination of Context–Mechanism–Outcome (CMO) configurations to investigate dissemination and adoption decision-making associated with a principles-based digital public health intervention. Rather than considering these findings independently, the sequential mixed-methods design generated complementary temporal, relational, and explanatory evidence that provided a more comprehensive understanding of dissemination than any individual analytical approach could achieve.

The findings demonstrated measurable engagement following the public release of the Violence Prevention Charter, followed by accelerated diffusion after implementation of a targeted promotional intervention. Consistent with Rogers’ Diffusion of Innovations theory, dissemination increased awareness and accelerated adoption through communication within a social system (2). Similarly, the Bass Diffusion Model (1) characterized the observed adoption pattern, demonstrating how innovation adoption progressed beyond initial uptake as dissemination activities expanded across the network. However, the subsequent phases of the investigation demonstrated that dissemination alone did not explain participant engagement. Social Network Analysis characterized the professional relationships through which information circulated within the PHABC network and participating partner organizations, while the realist-informed inquiry explained how participants interpreted the Charter within their own organizational contexts and why they chose to engage. Together, these complementary findings demonstrate that digital dissemination is best understood not as a single communication event but as a dynamic process shaped by interactions among communication, professional relationships, organizational context, and participant reasoning.

An important practical observation emerging from the investigation is that promotion requires promotion. Although the Charter generated measurable engagement following its public release, purposeful dissemination substantially accelerated adoption. This finding reinforces Rogers' (2) observation that communication is fundamental to innovation diffusion while extending it by demonstrating that communication alone is insufficient to explain adoption within contemporary digital public health environments. Dissemination established opportunities for engagement, but adoption reflected decisions made by individuals and organizations within existing professional relationships, organizational contexts, and shared public health values.

Importantly, no single method fully explained the dissemination process. Web analytics and diffusion modeling identified when engagement occurred and how adoption evolved over time. Social Network Analysis examined through whom information and influence circulated, while the realist-informed inquiry explained why participants chose to engage under differing contextual conditions. Considered together, these complementary methods provided a richer understanding of dissemination and adoption decision-making than any individual analytical approach could achieve. This integrated interpretation forms the foundation for the subsequent discussion of digital public health ecosystems, Complex Adaptive Systems, and the methodological contribution of the sequential mixed-methods framework.

### Digital ecosystems as settings for health promotion

The findings suggest that dissemination of the Violence Prevention Charter occurred within a broader digital public health ecosystem rather than through isolated communication channels. Information moved across multiple organizational and professional networks, participants interpreted shared principles according to their own organizational contexts, and decisions to engage reflected interactions among communication processes, professional relationships, organizational priorities, and individual reasoning. Rather than functioning solely as a communication platform, the digital environment served as a contemporary setting within which health promotion activities, collaboration, and organizational decision-making occurred.

This perspective extends the settings-based approach established in the Ottawa Charter for Health Promotion, which recognizes that health is created and experienced within the settings of everyday life. Increasingly, these settings include digitally connected environments where information, relationships, and social interaction influence health-related decision-making across multiple levels of the socio-ecological model. Within this investigation, the digital ecosystem provided an environment in which public health organizations exchanged information, interpreted shared principles, strengthened professional relationships, and voluntarily coordinated action around violence prevention. In this way, the digital environment functioned not simply as a dissemination tool, but as a setting that supported health promotion through communication, collaboration, and shared learning.

Recent scholarship further strengthens this interpretation. Kickbusch and Holly (37) argue that digital environments increasingly shape the social, political, commercial, and informational conditions that influence health and wellbeing, positioning digital ecosystems as important determinants of health rather than simply channels for communication. From this perspective, digital technologies influence how health information is created, shared, interpreted, and acted upon while simultaneously shaping the relationships and organizational networks through which public health practice occurs. Similarly, emerging scholarship in digital public health recognizes that digital ecosystems comprise interconnected social, organizational, and technological environments in which multiple actors interact, adapt, and exchange information in ways that influence public health action. The findings of the present study are consistent with this perspective, demonstrating that dissemination was influenced not only by communication reach but also by trust, organizational credibility, professional relationships, and contextual interpretation.

Importantly, these findings do not suggest that digital technologies themselves produce collaboration or behavior change. Rather, they demonstrate that digital ecosystems create opportunities for interaction within which existing professional relationships, organizational contexts, and participant reasoning influence dissemination and voluntary adoption. This distinction is important because it recognizes that technologies support—but do not determine—public health action. Instead, meaningful engagement emerged through interactions among communication processes, trusted professional relationships, organizational context, and shared public health values.

The principles-based design of the Violence Prevention Charter further illustrates this relationship. Rather than prescribing standardized implementation activities, the Charter encouraged organizations to interpret shared public health principles according to their own priorities, capacities, and community contexts. This flexibility enabled organizations to exercise professional judgement while remaining connected through a common set of violence prevention principles. Consistent with health promotion theory, the intervention therefore supported locally appropriate action rather than uniform implementation, reinforcing the importance of enabling environments that encourage participation, collaboration, and adaptation across diverse public health settings.

Taken together, these findings suggest that digital ecosystems should be understood as contemporary settings for health promotion in which dissemination, collaboration, and decision-making emerge through dynamic interactions among communication technologies, professional relationships, organizational contexts, and individual agency. Extending established health promotion theory into digitally connected environments provides a stronger conceptual foundation for understanding principles-based public health interventions and reinforces the value of investigating digital ecosystems as adaptive settings within which health promotion practice increasingly occurs.

### Independent decision-making within trusted social networks

The integration of findings across the sequential mixed-methods investigation provides important insight into how participants engaged with the Violence Prevention Charter. Temporal analyses demonstrated when engagement occurred and diffusion accelerated. Bass diffusion modeling characterized the pattern of adoption over time. Social Network Analysis described the relational pathways through which information and shared principles circulated within the PHABC network and participating partner organizations, while the realist-informed inquiry explained how participants interpreted the Charter within their own organizational contexts and why they chose to engage. Together, these complementary methods demonstrate that dissemination cannot be fully understood without considering both the relationships through which information travels and the contextual reasoning that influences adoption decisions.

Across these complementary analyses, one finding remained remarkably consistent: engagement occurred through trusted professional relationships rather than through communication exposure alone. The Social Network Analysis demonstrated high levels of trust, collaboration, and connectivity among organizations within the PHABC network, while the realist-informed inquiry identified confidence in participating organizations, credibility of the Charter, commitment to violence prevention, opportunities for collaboration, and alignment with shared public health values as mechanisms influencing participant engagement. Collectively, these findings suggest that dissemination reflected more than the transmission of information; it represented a process of professional interpretation occurring within established relationships characterized by trust and shared purpose.

Contemporary realist scholarship provides additional insight into this interpretation. Shaw et al. (34) emphasize that implementation outcomes emerge through the interaction between contextual conditions and participant reasoning rather than from intervention characteristics alone. Similarly, Jagosh (33) argues that realist inquiry is particularly valuable for understanding complex interventions because it seeks to explain how and why outcomes vary across different contexts rather than determining whether an intervention simply works. These perspectives closely align with the present findings, where participant engagement was influenced by how organizations interpreted the Violence Prevention Charter within their own mandates, priorities, capacities, and existing partnerships rather than by the Charter itself.

This interpretation is further supported by Flynn et al. (36), who demonstrated that variation in implementation frequently reflects differences in local organizational contexts and the mechanisms those contexts activate. Consistent with this perspective, the present investigation found that organizations were not passive recipients of information but active decision-makers who assessed the relevance of the Charter within their own environments. Shared public health principles provided a common foundation, while local organizational contexts influenced how those principles were interpreted and applied. The observed variation in engagement therefore reflects the adaptive nature of public health practice rather than inconsistency in the intervention itself.

Importantly, these findings should not be interpreted as suggesting that trusted relationships alone determine dissemination. Rather, trust functioned as one component within a broader network of interacting influences that included communication, organizational credibility, participant reasoning, and contextual opportunity. Decisions to endorse, promote, or implement the Charter reflected informed professional judgement supported by existing relationships and shared public health values. This interpretation is consistent with both diffusion theory and realist evaluation, while reinforcing the importance of understanding dissemination as a socially mediated and contextually situated process.

The findings also extend understanding of professional public health networks within digital environments. The Social Network Analysis demonstrated that relationships within the PHABC network provided the relational architecture through which information and influence circulated, while the realist-informed inquiry explained why those relationships contributed to participant engagement. Viewed together, these complementary findings suggest that effective digital dissemination depends not simply on expanding communication reach but on fostering trusted relationships that support professional dialogue, collaborative learning, and independent decision-making. Public health organizations may therefore achieve greater impact by strengthening existing networks and enabling meaningful engagement than by relying solely on increasingly sophisticated communication technologies.

### Understanding diffusion through a complex adaptive systems perspective

The integration of web analytics, Bass diffusion modeling, Social Network Analysis, and realist-informed inquiry generated complementary evidence describing different dimensions of the same dissemination process. No individual method was intended to explain the complexity of intervention diffusion independently. Rather, each contributed a distinct perspective that, when considered collectively, provided a more comprehensive understanding of dissemination and adoption decision-making within the PHABC network and participating partner organizations.

A Complex Adaptive Systems (CAS) perspective provides the most coherent framework for interpreting these integrated findings. Rather than conceptualizing dissemination as a linear communication process, CAS recognizes public health systems as dynamic networks of interacting individuals, organizations, and environments whose behaviors continually influence one another through feedback, adaptation, learning, and self-organization. From this perspective, dissemination is understood as an emergent process arising from multiple interacting relationships rather than a simple consequence of communication exposure alone.

Contemporary complexity scholarship reinforces this interpretation. Greenhalgh and Papoutsi (13) argue that health interventions should not be viewed as acting upon static organizational systems but as becoming embedded within adaptive networks of relationships that continually evolve through interaction, contextual adaptation, and learning. This perspective recognizes that interventions both influence and are influenced by the systems in which they operate. The findings of the present study are consistent with this interpretation. Diffusion modeling described the temporal dynamics of dissemination, Social Network Analysis characterized the relational architecture through which information and influence circulated, and the realist-informed inquiry explained how contextual conditions and participant reasoning shaped engagement. Together, these complementary findings illustrate how multiple interacting processes contributed to dissemination within a digital public health ecosystem.

Importantly, this study does not claim to demonstrate complexity empirically or to provide direct evidence of emergence or system transformation. Rather, the observed patterns are consistent with a Complex Adaptive Systems perspective that offers a coherent explanatory framework for interpreting the converging evidence generated through the sequential mixed-methods investigation. This distinction is important because the study was designed to investigate dissemination and adoption decision-making, not to measure the behavior of the system itself. The value of the CAS perspective therefore lies in its ability to explain how communication processes, professional relationships, organizational context, and participant reasoning interacted to influence dissemination across the network.

The findings also reinforce the importance of agency within complex systems. Organizations did not respond uniformly to the Violence Prevention Charter, nor were they expected to. Instead, participants interpreted shared violence prevention principles according to their own organizational mandates, priorities, partnerships, and community contexts. These locally informed decisions contributed to the overall dissemination process while preserving organizational autonomy. Such adaptive responses are consistent with principles of health promotion and complexity science, where locally situated decision-making is understood to strengthen rather than diminish system resilience and innovation.

Viewed collectively, the findings suggest that dissemination of principles-based public health interventions is best understood as an adaptive process operating within a complex digital ecosystem. Communication created opportunities for engagement, professional networks facilitated the circulation of information and influence, organizational contexts shaped interpretation, and participant reasoning informed adoption decisions. The sequential integration of temporal, relational, and explanatory evidence therefore provides a richer understanding of dissemination than any individual methodological approach alone and demonstrates the value of interpreting digital public health interventions through a Complex Adaptive Systems perspective.

### Methodological contribution

The principal methodological contribution of this investigation lies not in the individual application of web analytics, Bass diffusion modeling, Social Network Analysis (SNA), or realist-informed inquiry, but in their deliberate sequential integration. Each method examined a complementary dimension of dissemination and adoption decision-making. Web analytics and diffusion modeling characterized the temporal dynamics of dissemination, Social Network Analysis examined the relational architecture through which information and influence circulated within the PHABC network and participating partner organizations, and the realist-informed inquiry explained the contextual conditions and generative mechanisms that influenced participant engagement. Considered together, these methods generated complementary temporal, relational, and explanatory evidence describing the same adaptive phenomenon.

The sequential mixed-methods design extends existing approaches to evaluating digital public health interventions by recognizing that no single methodological perspective adequately explains dissemination within complex organizational environments. Digital public health interventions increasingly operate within systems characterized by multiple interacting actors, decentralized decision-making, evolving communication pathways, and diverse organizational contexts. Investigating these interventions therefore requires approaches capable of examining not only dissemination outcomes but also the relationships, contextual influences, and decision-making processes through which adoption occurs.

From a public health informatics perspective, the findings reinforce the value of integrating complementary analytical methods to investigate digital public health interventions. Public health informatics has increasingly emphasized understanding the interactions among people, information, technology, and organizational systems to improve public health practice and decision-making (38–40). While web analytics, network analysis, and implementation evaluation each provide valuable but distinct forms of evidence, their deliberate integration offers a more comprehensive understanding of dissemination than any individual method alone. The present investigation demonstrates how quantitative measures of dissemination can be strengthened through complementary relational and explanatory analyses, providing a richer understanding of how digital public health interventions are communicated, interpreted, and adopted within professional public health networks.

The methodological contribution also extends contemporary implementation science by demonstrating the value of combining diffusion theory, network science, and realist-informed inquiry within a single investigative sequence. Rather than privileging one methodological perspective, the sequential design acknowledges that complex public health interventions generate multiple forms of evidence, each contributing unique insight into dissemination and adoption decision-making. This integrated approach is consistent with calls for more pluralistic methodological frameworks capable of investigating complexity within health systems while remaining grounded in empirical observation (13, 33).

The principal contribution of this investigation therefore lies in demonstrating a sequential mixed-methods framework capable of integrating temporal, relational, and explanatory evidence within a single coherent analysis. Beyond the Violence Prevention Charter, this framework offers a transferable approach for investigating dissemination and adoption decision-making associated with principles-based digital public health interventions operating within complex adaptive systems. More broadly, it contributes to the methodological foundations of digital public health, public health informatics, and implementation science by illustrating how complementary analytical approaches can be integrated to investigate increasingly complex public health challenges.

### Implications for public health practice

Several practical implications emerge from this investigation for the design and implementation of principles-based digital public health interventions.

First, the findings reinforce that promotion requires promotion. Although the Violence Prevention Charter generated measurable engagement following its public release, purposeful dissemination substantially accelerated adoption. Simply making digital resources publicly available is unlikely to maximize awareness or engagement without deliberate communication strategies that promote visibility across professional networks. For public health organizations, dissemination should therefore be viewed as an active process requiring ongoing communication rather than a single publication event.

Second, the findings highlight the importance of trusted professional relationships in supporting dissemination and adoption. Communication reach alone did not explain participant engagement. Rather, organizations chose to engage because the Charter aligned with shared public health values, was introduced through credible professional relationships, and could be interpreted within their own organizational mandates and community contexts. These findings suggest that dissemination strategies are likely to be more effective when they build upon existing networks of trust and collaboration than when they rely exclusively on increasingly sophisticated communication technologies or broad messaging campaigns.

Third, the findings demonstrate the value of principles-based public health interventions for addressing complex public health issues. Rather than prescribing standardized implementation activities, the Violence Prevention Charter encouraged organizations to interpret and apply shared violence prevention principles according to their own priorities, capacities, and community needs. This flexibility supported locally appropriate responses while maintaining alignment with common public health objectives. Such an approach reflects established principles of health promotion by enabling organizations to exercise professional judgement while contributing to broader collective goals.

More broadly, the findings suggest that digital public health interventions should be designed with equal attention to communication, relationships, organizational context, and participant reasoning. Effective dissemination depends not only on communicating information but also on creating opportunities for meaningful interaction, collaboration, and shared learning within trusted professional networks. Understanding digital ecosystems as contemporary settings for health promotion therefore encourages a shift from viewing technology as the intervention itself to recognizing technology as part of a broader environment that supports collaboration, knowledge exchange, and adaptive public health practice.

Finally, the sequential mixed-methods framework demonstrated in this investigation offers practical value beyond evaluation alone. By integrating temporal, relational, and explanatory evidence, the framework provides public health practitioners and researchers with a structured approach for understanding not only whether dissemination occurs, but how, through whom, and why adoption decisions are made. This broader understanding may support the design, implementation, and evaluation of future digital public health initiatives operating within increasingly complex organizational environments.

### Limitations and future research

The findings should be interpreted within the context and purpose of this investigation. This study examined dissemination and adoption decision-making associated with a principles-based violence prevention intervention within the PHABC network and participating partner organizations. As a sequential mixed-methods case study, the objective was not to establish causal relationships or produce findings intended for statistical generalization. Rather, the investigation sought to develop a richer understanding of dissemination by integrating complementary temporal, relational, and explanatory forms of evidence within a single analytical framework. The intention was to generate an empirically grounded explanation of dissemination and adoption decision-making that may inform understanding of similar public health interventions while recognizing that the transferability of these findings depends upon the characteristics of the settings in which they are applied.

Several methodological considerations should therefore be acknowledged. First, the investigation examined a single principles-based intervention operating within one bounded digital public health ecosystem. Although the findings provide detailed insight into dissemination and adoption decision-making within this context, other public health priorities, organizational structures, digital environments, and professional networks may demonstrate different patterns of dissemination and engagement. Rather than seeking universal explanation, the study contributes contextually grounded knowledge that may be transferable to other settings where similar conditions, relationships, and implementation approaches exist.

Second, each methodological component contributed insight into a distinct dimension of dissemination while also possessing inherent limitations when considered independently. Web analytics and diffusion modeling characterized patterns of engagement over time but could not explain why individuals or organizations chose to engage. Social Network Analysis described the relational architecture of the PHABC network and participating partner organizations but did not determine how relationships influenced participant reasoning or organizational decision-making. Conversely, the realist-informed inquiry provided explanatory insight into contextual influences and generative mechanisms but was not intended to quantify the relative contribution of individual mechanisms or predict dissemination outcomes. The deliberate sequential integration of these complementary methods was therefore central to the investigative design, allowing the strengths of one approach to inform, extend, and explain the findings of the others.

Third, although Complex Adaptive Systems provided a coherent explanatory framework for interpreting the integrated findings, the investigation was not designed to measure system behavior directly or demonstrate emergence empirically. Rather, the observed dissemination patterns were interpreted as being consistent with a Complex Adaptive Systems perspective. This distinction is important because it positions complexity as a theoretical framework through which complementary evidence can be understood rather than as an outcome measured by the investigation itself. Maintaining this distinction strengthens the interpretation by ensuring that conclusions remain aligned with the scope of the empirical evidence.

The principles-based nature of the Violence Prevention Charter should also be considered when interpreting the findings. Unlike interventions that prescribe standardized implementation activities, the Charter encouraged organizations to interpret and apply shared principles according to their own priorities, capacities, and community contexts. Variation in organizational responses was therefore anticipated and reflects an important characteristic of principles-based health promotion interventions rather than inconsistency in implementation. The findings should consequently be interpreted as demonstrating how organizations exercised independent professional judgement within shared public health principles rather than evaluating adherence to a prescribed implementation model.

These methodological boundaries also identify important opportunities for future research. Application of the sequential mixed-methods framework across different public health interventions, organizational settings, and digital ecosystems would strengthen understanding of its transferability and methodological utility. Longitudinal investigations could examine how dissemination, collaboration, and organizational learning evolve over time, while comparative studies may explore how differing network structures, governance arrangements, and organizational contexts influence adoption decision-making. Additional research examining digital ecosystems as contemporary settings for health promotion would further advance understanding of how communication technologies, professional relationships, adaptive organizational systems, and contextual influences interact to shape public health practice.

Ultimately, the methodological boundaries of the individual analytical approaches reinforce one of the principal contributions of this investigation. No single method fully explained dissemination and adoption decision-making within this complex public health environment. By deliberately integrating temporal, relational, and explanatory forms of evidence, the sequential mixed-methods design provided a more comprehensive understanding of dissemination than any individual analytical approach could have achieved independently. This integrated investigative framework therefore offers a transferable approach for future research seeking to understand the complexity of digital public health interventions operating within adaptive organizational systems.

## Conclusion

This investigation contributes a sequential mixed-methods framework for understanding dissemination and adoption decision-making associated with principles-based digital public health interventions. By integrating web analytics, Bass diffusion modeling, Social Network Analysis, and a realist-informed examination of Context–Mechanism–Outcome (CMO) configurations, the study generated complementary temporal, relational, and explanatory evidence describing how dissemination occurred, through whom information and influence travelled, and why individuals and organizations chose to engage.

Interpreted through a Complex Adaptive Systems perspective, the findings suggest that dissemination within digital public health ecosystems is shaped not only by communication processes but also by interactions among professional relationships, organizational context, participant reasoning, and shared public health values. The investigation demonstrates that purposeful dissemination accelerated adoption, while trusted professional networks and locally situated decision-making influenced how organizations interpreted and applied shared violence prevention principles. These findings reinforce the importance of understanding dissemination as an adaptive process operating within contemporary digital ecosystems rather than as a linear sequence of communication events.

The study also advances the conceptualization of digital ecosystems as contemporary settings for health promotion. Rather than functioning solely as channels for information exchange, digital environments provided settings in which organizations collaborated, interpreted shared principles, and independently determined appropriate courses of action within their own communities and organizational contexts. Understanding digital ecosystems in this way extends established health promotion theory while providing a stronger conceptual foundation for investigating digital public health interventions.

The principal contribution of this research lies not in the individual application of diffusion modeling, Social Network Analysis, or realist-informed inquiry, but in demonstrating how these complementary methods can be deliberately integrated within a sequential mixed-methods investigative framework. By combining temporal, relational, and explanatory forms of evidence, the framework provides a richer understanding of dissemination and adoption decision-making than any individual analytical approach alone. Beyond the Violence Prevention Charter, this investigative framework offers a transferable approach for future research examining principles-based interventions operating within complex public health systems.

As digital technologies become increasingly embedded within public health practice, understanding how information, relationships, organizational context, and participant reasoning interact to influence dissemination will become increasingly important. This investigation contributes to the growing fields of digital public health, public health informatics, implementation science, and health promotion by providing an empirically grounded framework for investigating dissemination within contemporary digital public health ecosystems.
